title: Deborah, Barak, and Jael Defeat Sisera
summary: Israel falls under Jabin, a Canaanite king of Hazor whose commander Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, a prophet who is judging Israel, summons Barak to lead ten thousand men to Mount Tabor, and when he will not go without her she tells him the honor will go to a woman. The LORD routs Sisera's army at the Kishon, and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, who kills him with a tent peg as he sleeps.
story: After Ehud's long rest, the cycle turns again, and this time the oppression comes from inside the land itself: a Canaanite king in the north, the kind of enemy chapter 1 said the tribes had failed to drive out. This is one of the book's clearest victories, and it is told twice, first in this prose account and then in the poetry of chapter 5. It stands near the high point of the judges before the long decline that begins with Gideon. It is also a story about who gets the credit. The judge is a woman, the reluctant general is a man, and the decisive blow is struck by a foreign woman in a tent.
historical:
Hazor, in upper Galilee north of the Sea of Galilee, was the largest city in Canaan in the second millennium BC, and excavations there (led by Yigael Yadin in the 1950s and later by Amnon Ben-Tor) have uncovered a huge city destroyed by fire in the Late Bronze Age. Joshua 11 records that Joshua burned Hazor and killed its king, also named Jabin. How this relates to Judges 4 is debated. Some suggest Jabin was a dynastic name used by more than one king, and that Hazor recovered for a time; others think the two accounts describe the same events from different traditions; others see the Jabin of Judges as a later ruler of a rebuilt city. The book calls him king of Canaan, suggesting a leader of a coalition of northern cities.

The battle was fought in the Jezreel Valley, the broad plain between Galilee and the hills of Samaria, drained by the River Kishon. Chariots were the ancient world's advanced military technology, fast and terrifying on flat, dry ground. Mount Tabor, a rounded hill rising steeply from the plain, gave Barak's infantry a place where chariots could not reach them. Harosheth-hagoyim, Sisera's base, has not been identified with certainty. The song in chapter 5 adds that the Kishon swept the enemy away, suggesting a sudden storm turned the plain to mud and made the chariots useless.
cultural:
Deborah held court under a palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim, where Israelites came to her for judgment, meaning decisions in disputes. She is also called a prophetess, one who speaks the word of God, like Miriam before her (Exodus 15:20) and Huldah after her (2 Kings 22:14). Her description as the wife of Lappidoth may also be read as woman of torches or woman of fire, since lappidoth means torches, though most translations take it as her husband's name. Barak's name means lightning.

The Kenites were a nomadic clan related to Moses' in-laws (Hobab here, elsewhere Jethro or Reuel). Heber had separated from them and made peace with Jabin, perhaps working as a metalsmith for the Canaanites, since the name Kenite may be connected with smithing, though that is uncertain. In the ancient Near East, hospitality was a sacred duty, and a guest in one's tent was under protection. It was also true that a woman's tent was her own space, where no man other than her husband would normally enter. Sisera's choice to hide there and Jael's act both violate expectations. Setting up and taking down tents was usually women's work among nomads, so Jael handled the peg and mallet with practiced skill.
literary: The narrative is built around the question of honor. Deborah's words in verse 9 set up suspense: the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. A first-time reader assumes she means Deborah herself, and only later discovers it is Jael. The battle itself takes only a few verses, and the narrator makes it clear that the LORD routed Sisera (verse 15), echoing the language of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:24). The pace then slows dramatically in Jael's tent: the invitation, the blanket, the milk, the instruction to lie, the sleep, the peg. There are layers of irony. Sisera asks Jael to say no man is there, and in a sense he is right: the great commander has been reduced to nothing. The chapter closes with two summary verses (23 and 24) that give the credit to God and describe the eventual destruction of Jabin.

outline.t: Israel sold to Jabin of Hazor
Deborah summons Barak, who will not go alone
Heber the Kenite pitches his tent near Kedesh
The LORD routs Sisera's army at the Kishon
Jael kills Sisera in her tent
God subdues Jabin king of Canaan

doctrines.note: The LORD draws Sisera to the Kishon, routs his army, and subdues Jabin. The nine hundred iron chariots that terrified Israel prove powerless against him.
Deborah speaks the word of the LORD, and it comes true in detail, including the surprising word about a woman. God guides his people through prophetic speech.

God works through the unlikely: a woman judge, a hesitant commander, a Kenite family at peace with the enemy, and a tent peg. His purposes are carried out through people who may not even belong to Israel.

words.note: Nevi'ah, prophetess, the feminine form of the word for prophet. Deborah is one of only a few women in the Old Testament given this title. Her authority to summon Barak rests on the word of God she speaks, not on military rank.

Hamam, to throw into confusion or panic. The same verb describes how the LORD threw the Egyptian army into confusion at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:24). The echo presents Sisera's defeat as a new exodus, a divine rout of a chariot army.

Rekhev, chariot. The word appears again and again, and the nine hundred iron chariots are the measure of Israel's fear. The story's point is that God's power makes them useless, and Sisera ends up fleeing on foot.
Kana, to be humbled or subdued. On that day God subdued Jabin (verse 23). The verb gives the victory its true author: not Barak, not Deborah, not Jael, but God.

christ: Deborah's song and story show God defeating a far stronger enemy through unlikely instruments, a pattern that runs through Scripture and comes to its fullest expression in the cross, where God defeated evil through apparent weakness (1 Corinthians 1:25). Some Christian readers have noticed that Jael crushes the enemy's head, and have connected it to the promise in Genesis 3:15 that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head. Others think that link is too loose, since Genesis speaks of the woman's offspring, not the woman herself. Barak is named among the heroes of faith in Hebrews 11:32. The connection to Christ is thematic: a victory won by God for a people who could not win it themselves.

hard.q: Is Jael a hero or a murderer, and why does Scripture praise her?
hard.a: Jael invited Sisera in, told him not to fear, gave him milk, and then killed him as he slept, which violated the sacred code of hospitality and her household's peace with Jabin. Chapter 5 calls her most blessed of women. Some interpreters defend her as acting in wartime against a brutal enemy commander who had oppressed Israel for twenty years, choosing the side of God's people at great risk to herself. Others emphasize that Scripture records her act and the song celebrates Israel's deliverance without offering a full moral assessment of her methods. Still others note that Sisera's own entry into a woman's tent was a violation, and that he asked her to lie. Readers across these views agree that the text presents Sisera's death as the outworking of God's word in verse 9, while leaving the ethics of the act for the reader to weigh.

questions: Barak would not go without Deborah. Was that faith, weakness, or both? What do you need before you will obey God?
God used a woman judge, a hesitant general, and a foreign woman to deliver Israel. What does that suggest about whom God is willing to use?
What are the iron chariots in your life, the things that seem too strong to overcome?
